articles.title_zh: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 22, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
The Kremlin’s seeming interest in negotiations aims not to end the war in Ukraine but rather to secure economic concessions from the United States such that Russia can continue funding its war. Various Russian officials tried to present the October 21 meeting between US Special Representative to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin as evidence that Russia is willing to engage in meaningful negotiations to end the war while simultaneously attempting to extract economic concessions from the United States so that Russia can continue funding the war.[1] Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev, for example, claimed on October 21 that Witkoff and Putin used the October 21 meeting to agree to expand Russian-US economic cooperation and to “continue communicating.”[2] A Kremlin domestic policy official told Russian opposition source Verstka that the Kremlin does not expect negotiations to resolve the war in Ukraine but that Russian officials hope to extract economic concessions, which could boost Russia’s budget and give Russia a military advantage.[3]
Other Russian officials meanwhile demonstrated Russia’s unwillingness to make any meaningful concessions toward ending the war in Ukraine. Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated on October 22 that Putin did not present any Russian peace proposal to Witkoff during their meeting and that Putin has not considered the composition of a potential Russian delegation for a future Russia-US-Ukraine trilateral meeting.[4] Russian State Duma deputies expressed skepticism on October 21 and 22 that negotiations could end the war and reiterated claims that freezing the current frontlines would be detrimental to Russia’s own efforts to end the war.[5] A source close to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) told Verstka on October 22 that the Kremlin has been working for over 1.5 years to try to sway the Trump administration to Russia’s side and that the Kremlin’s current negotiation efforts are emphasizing Ukraine’s alleged hopelessness. These are similar to the Kremlin’s earlier negotiation tactics which tried to convince the United States and the West generally that Ukrainian defenses were going to collapse such that Ukraine should preemptively capitulate.[6]
The Kremlin is fundamentally interested only in buying time to resolve the war on the battlefield while Russia simultaneously reaps the benefits of economic cooperation with the United States. State Duma Defense Committee First Deputy Chairperson Alexei Zhuravlyov stated on October 21 that Russia must “press” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the battlefield and force Ukraine to “capitulate.”[7] Zhuravlyov added that Russia should not rely on diplomacy with the United States because Russian “successes on the ground” will strengthen Russia’s negotiating position.[8] Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov similarly claimed that Russian forces maintain the “complete strategic initiative” and are conducting a “relentless offensive” in all key areas of the frontline.[9]
Russian forces are not winning on the battlefield, however, particularly as Ukrainian forces have stymied the planned Russian offensive to seize Donetsk Oblast. ISW has observed evidence that Russian forces suffered a net loss of 241 square kilometers of territory in Ukraine since September 1, 2026. The average rate of daily Russian advances has significantly declined since 2025, with an average of 0.25 square kilometers per day so far in 2026. Ukrainian forces have, comparatively, been contesting and seizing the operational initiative across several sectors of the frontline throughout 2026, including most recently in the Lyman direction with Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi which liberated over 270 square kilometers of territory and thwarted the Russian military command’s plan to encircle the Fortress Belt.[10] Russian forces are also facing mounting monthly casualties while the Russian recruitment rate continues to fall short of its loss rate.[11] Russian forces have suffered almost 37,000 casualties thus far in October 2026 — much higher than the 31,270 casualties for all of October 2025.[12] The Kremlin may face mounting challenges in the coming months, should Ukraine continue to contest the operational initiative and disrupt Russian offensive plans, potentially further pushing Russian commanders to urge Putin to conduct a mobilization in some form.[13]
The Kremlin is likely actively seeking economic cooperation with the United States as Russia faces significant financial strain. Sources familiar with the matter told Bloomberg on October 22 that even a few more months of continued war could exact lasting financial damage on Russian state-owned oil company Rosneft, as Ukrainian strikes against Rosneft’s oil refineries have significantly reduced the company’s profits and increased its debt.[14] Bloomberg added that repeated Ukrainian strikes have prevented Rosneft from completing repairs and restarting refinery operations and that strikes against complex secondary units that often include Western-sourced parts, like catalytic crackers, reformers, and hydrocrackers, are particularly difficult to repair. Russia remains highly susceptible to international sanctions that restrict its access to the technologically advanced components needed to repair the equipment damaged after Ukraine’s strikes.[15] The Kremlin is therefore pushing the United States for various forms of economic relief, so that Russia can continue funding its war against Ukraine.[16] The Kremlin has continuously sought to extract economic concessions during negotiations to alleviate the pressure on its oil industry — including restrictions on Ukrainian strikes against refineries and the relaxation of US sanctions against diesel exports — while expressing little real interest in ending the war.[17]
Russian forces conducted a massive missile and drone strike against Ukraine overnight on October 21 to 22 following the October 21 meeting between Witkoff and Putin — a continuation of Russia’s pattern of launching large strike packages in the days before and after major peace talks. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces conducted a massive combined missile and drone strike primarily targeting Kyiv City and using an unspecified number of Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles and 210 long-range drones, 110 of which were jet-powered.[18] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russian forces conducted three waves of ballistic missile strikes against Kyiv City using 21 missiles, damaging residential, energy, railway, and commercial infrastructure.[19] Zelensky stated that Russian strikes targeted 12 Ukrainian oblasts, killing at least two people and injuring at least 34 people. Russian forces regularly conduct massive strikes in the days right before and after bilateral and trilateral talks, such as the August 2025 US-Russia Alaska summit, the November 2025 US-Ukraine talks in Geneva, the November 2025 US-Russia talks in Moscow, the December 2025 US-Ukrainian-European and US-Russian talks, and the January-February 2026 US-Ukrainian-Russian talks in Abu Dhabi.[20]
Russian forces struck Kyiv City with cluster munitions to purposely harm the civilian population, likely as part of wider Russian efforts to distract from Ukraine’s recent battlefield successes and ultimately force Ukraine into capitulation by making daily life untenable. Zelensky stated that Russian forces struck Pechersk Raion, the historic center of Kyiv City, with three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads that have a dispersion diameter of 400 meters.[21] The strikes damaged monastery buildings and other civilian infrastructure near the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Presentation Monastery. articles.title_orig: Capcom Data Breach Results In Unauthorised Access To More Than 11.7 Million 'CAPCOM ID' Accounts
articles.title_zh: Capcom Data Breach Results In Unauthorised Access To More Than 11.7 Million 'CAPCOM ID' Accounts
articles.content_orig:
Japanese gaming giant Capcom has confirmed that hackers breached its membership service, CAPCOM ID, exposing more than 11.7 million customer email addresses and associated information.
Apart from emails, exposed data includes account creation date, last login timestamp, number of logins, and the IP address used at the last login.
Capcom found that for a small subset of 43 accounts, dates of birth, gender, nicknames, and countries were also exposed.
For another subset of 196 accounts, the hackers changed the CAPCOM ID login passwords in an attempt to lock the owners out, but the company took action and reset them.
In an alert today , the gaming company says that passwords for all other registered members have not been exposed and that credit card information remained unaffected.
Capcom is a Japanese video game developer and publisher known for franchises such as Resident Evil, Monster Hunter, Street Fighter, and Mega Man. The company has 4,000 employees and an annual revenue of $1.24 billion.
CAPCOM ID is the company’s shared account system used for accessing its web services and playing some of its online games.
Although the timing of the breach remains unclear, Capcom said it detected suspicious activity and confirmed unauthorized access on October 19.
An investigation was launched immediately, and by the following day, it was clear that customer information had been compromised.
October 21, the company reported the  incident to the police and to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.
Capcom said its online services remain unaffected, but cautioned users to stay vigilant for unsolicited communications and emails requesting additional information, or messages containing URLs and attachments.
During the investigation, Capcom identified the intrusion method and implemented security measures to prevent similar incidents. However, no details related to the initial access have been shared.
The gaming firm also says it will notify affected customers in stages, likely due to the large volume of affected accounts, but it has established region-specific communication channels to submit support requests.
In November 2020, Capcom suffered an attack claimed by the Ragnar Locker ransomware gang , in which attackers claimed to have stolen 1 TB of data . The company subsequently warned that up to 390,000 people could be affected.
In April 2021, Capcom disclosed that the attackers had gained access through an old VPN device .
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

A large clinical trial combining Moderna 's mRNA cancer vaccine with Merck 's immunotherapy reduced the risk of melanoma death or recurrence by 42%, the companies announced on Thursday, potentially opening a new era in personalized oncology.
Moderna shares closed more than 17% lower on Thursday after the trial findings leaked on an oncology website, despite having nearly quadrupled through Wednesday's close since August when the trial's success was first announced without full data. Merck stock also fell about 1.8%.
The Phase 3 trial, which tracked more than 1,100 patients, also revealed that the combination treatment reduced the risk of the cancer spreading by 38%.
The findings mark the first data demonstrating that pairing a custom vaccine based on a patient's unique tumor mutations with a drug that boosts the immune system can successfully halt the disease. The vaccine was tested alongside Merck's Keytruda, one of the world's top-selling medicines.
Keytruda functions by removing a natural brake that cancer cells rely on to hide from immune attack. Meanwhile, the vaccine instructs patient cells to produce copies of specific mutations, allowing the immune system to seek out and destroy them.
Moderna CEO Stephane Bancel stated that the findings herald a new chapter in treating cancer.
"With this ability to create new T cells that are specific to your tumor... the clinical impact is very profound, and as we saw in the Phase 2 (trial), very lasting," Bancel said in an interview.
The companies are preparing to file for US regulatory approval, expecting to launch the personalized cancer vaccine in 2027, Bancel noted.
The results, evaluating patient outcomes over the initial two years following treatment, are scheduled for presentation on Saturday at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference in Madrid.
Among subjects who received the vaccine paired with Keytruda, 82.2% remained cancer-free after two years, compared to 70% of those who received Keytruda alone.
"This is highly statistically significant. It is not by chance," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
Ahead of the meeting, several Wall Street analysts noted that investors were looking for the combination to cut the risk of recurrence by 40% or more.
"There appears to be a sell-on-the-news reaction playing out here," William Blair analyst Myles Minter wrote in a research note, pointing out that Moderna shares remained up 525% this year even with Thursday's downward move.
Minter added that the findings were "great data, in our view, but investors will continue to debate the fundamental valuation."
The trial assessed nine doses of the vaccine, known as intismeran, administered with Keytruda beginning 13 weeks after surgery to remove melanoma lesions, comparing responses against the standard single-therapy treatment of Keytruda alone.

Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices.
The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
"It is a flight to safety," said Mitch Goldberg, president of ClientFirst Strategy. "People are all of a sudden terrified of the amount of bond issuance by AI-related companies. They see the rates going up and people want to hold on to something that they think will be there at maturity."
Others on Wall Street also sought to explain the turnaround in bond prices.
"For the first time in a while, Treasurys are enjoying haven status," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds. "You have weakness in tech, an escalation of risk in the Middle East and higher oil. On a relative basis Treasurys start to look like the safe place to hide again in the short term."
The reversal in bonds this week emerged as questions persisted about the billions being spent to build artificial intelligence networks.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that while demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ," capital was scarce. Neoclouds are a specialized cloud computing providers that focus on high-performance tech infrastructure designed specifically for artificial intelligence.
This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades amid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices.
Above 5%, however, attitudes began to shift and yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%.
Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday. Oil prices moved sharply higher, with West Texas Intermediate futures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel. Brent crude futures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel.
Higher energy prices followed a New York Times report, citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"You always look for one risk point, and there isn't really just one at the moment, which makes it a little bit more challenging," said Gregory Faranello, head of U.S. macro strategy at South Street Securities. "But if I had to take one of those and say what's most important right now, it has to be what's going on geopolitically."
"The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. If energy prices "stay elevated, it could force the Fed's hand to do even more, which certainly wouldn't be wouldn't be a good thing for the bond market."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Injuries in China's Tibet rise to 65 after earthquake, death toll remains at 16
articles.title_zh: Injuries in China's Tibet rise to 65 after earthquake, death toll remains at 16
articles.content_orig:
At least 16 people have died and dozens were injured after a magnitude 7 earthquake struck Tibet on Thursday, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
The epicenter was 183 kilometers East-Northeast of the city of Nagqu in the Tibet region, according to the United States Geological Survey.
At least 339 houses have collapsed and the extent of the damage is still being assessed, according to Xinhua. A rescue team has been dispatched to the epicenter.
Railway authorities have suspended train services through the affected areas, according to state media CCTV.
The China Earthquake Administration has activated a level II emergency response, its second-highest tier, Chinese broadcaster CGTN said.
In villages near the epicenter, authorities have found at least two injured people and houses with visible cracks, Reuters reported citing a state broadcaster.
Videos released by local media showed people leaving their homes as the quake struck, Reuters reported.
The average elevation within a 5-kilometer radius of the epicenter exceeds 4,800 meters, according to the China Earthquake Networks Center.
China is no stranger to powerful quakes, especially in southwestern parts of the country where the Eurasian tectonic plate meets the Indian plate, a dramatic collision that creates the mighty Himalayas and the vast Tibetan plateau.
Thursday’s earthquake comes roughly two months after the catastrophic flooding disaster on the edge of the Tibetan plateau on the border with Nepal, that was sparked by a huge glacier collapse and landslide. It killed at least 1,300 people and left more than 5,000 missing.
The last comparably-strong earthquake to rock China occurred in January 2024, when a 7.1-magnitude quake hit a mountainous and remote part of China’s far western Xinjiang region, killing three people and injuring scores more.
In December 2023, over one hundred people were killed when an earthquake hit China’s Jishishan county in Gansu province, northwest China, making it the country’s deadliest in nearly a decade.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: Blaze that killed 4 soldiers on Canadian military base sparked on grenade launcher range, officials say
articles.title_zh: Blaze that killed 4 soldiers on Canadian military base sparked on grenade launcher range, officials say
articles.content_orig:
A blaze that killed four soldiers and injured several dozen more on a military base in the Canadian province of Alberta last week broke out on a grenade launcher range during training exercises, officials said Thursday.
The fire sparked Oct. 17 on the automatic grenade launcher range of Canadian Forces Base Wainwright "during routine military training activities," Brig. Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal, said in a statement Thursday.
The fire initially remained within the range's "Permanent Danger Area 2," which limited the ability of firefighters to battle it directly, Hanrahan said, and crews were forced to monitor it throughout the day instead.
However, it then spread due to "a subsequent change in wind direction and velocity" that "significantly increased the fire's intensity and rate of speed which led to these tragic events," Hanrahan added.
There was no indication that natural gas infrastructure was involved in the fire, she disclosed.
The fire killed four soldiers and injured 39 others. The Canadian Armed Forces said Thursday that 27 soldiers remained hospitalized, while 12 had been treated and released.
Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that the fire was "driven by ferocious winds" and "jumped nearly a kilometer in less than a minute to where soldiers were gathered."
Carney said that 50 investigators had been brought in to probe the fire. The Canadian Forces National Investigation Service was leading the investigation, with support from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
"We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy, as expeditiously and transparently as necessary," Carney told reporters Monday.
The fire overtook soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, and Army reservists conducting live-fire training.
Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said Sunday that military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained and allowed training to continue before winds suddenly shifted.
About 84 soldiers from Charlie Company were training at two locations, one for throwing grenades and another for practicing attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second area.
Carney said the soldiers were preparing for a mission next spring to reinforce Canadian troops serving with NATO in Latvia.
Rutland said investigators would examine whether winds drove the flames toward the soldiers or whether the fire spread unseen through vegetation. They will also examine whether military safety procedures need to change, he said.
The military identified those killed as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Pvt. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, British Columbia; and Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, British Columbia.

articles.title_orig: You Should Enable This Chrome Feature That Flags Suspicious Websites
articles.title_zh: You Should Enable This Chrome Feature That Flags Suspicious Websites
articles.content_orig:
Emily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel.
In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET . Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
If you use Google Chrome, you can turn on a new safety feature that will warn you if you navigate to a suspicious website that looks like others already known for malicious behavior. The alerts are part of Enhanced Protection mode in Chrome's Safe Browsing, which checks your activity against potentially harmful sites and warns you if you're at risk of encountering malware, phishing, intrusive ads, or social engineering attacks.
Most internet users are familiar with the full-page alerts that appear if you navigate to a site that's known to be malicious. These red "dangerous site" warnings indicate a high risk of harm to the user and can't really be ignored since they take up the entire screen and urge you to go back to safety.
The new "suspicious site" alerts indicate possible risk of harm based on patterns consistent with other known malicious sites. This means that Google isn't as confident that the website is actually dangerous, but it looks a lot like others that are spreading malware or running phishing scams. These suspicious site warnings are smaller pop-ups with the text "This site doesn't seem right" and two button options: Mark as safe or Back to safety . The different colors, text, and formatting make it easy for users to distinguish between what Google deems dangerous versus suspicious.
Safe Browsing in Chrome has three options: standard protection, enhanced protection, and no protection at all (which isn't recommended). Standard protection checks your browsing activity, extensions, and downloads against Google's list of unsafe sites, which is updated periodically. By contrast, enhanced protection works in real time and uses AI analysis. Note that enhanced protection does require you to share more information about your activity to Google, and the data are linked to your Google Account.
While privacy-conscious users may be hesitant to send more info to Google, enhanced protection is likely worthwhile for those who aren't as savvy to advanced scam tactics (and therefore more likely to enter credentials or financial information on or download a file from a malicious website). To enable Enhanced Protection and receive suspicious website warnings, go to Settings > Privacy and security in Chrome and toggle Enhanced protection on under the Safe Browsing section.
Emily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Chris LaCivita and James Blair donate full Bosnian consulting fee to Trump presidential library
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Chris LaCivita and James Blair donate full Bosnian consulting fee to Trump presidential library
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Trump’s election advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair have donated their six-figure consulting fees from a controversial side-hustle in Bosnia and Herzegovina to Trump’s presidential library, The Post has learned.
Trump was “gloating” and “very braggadocious” in private conversations this week upon learning the development, a source said — indicating that his initial hard feelings toward LaCivita and Blair over their Eastern European gig had eased.
Another source confirmed Trump was pleased to hear of the donation.
The transfer was confirmed by four sources, two of whom said that Trump heard indirectly and not from the men about their decision.
LaCivita, who co-led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, and Blair, who served as a deputy chief of staff at the White House until May, likely will still have to pay income taxes on the revenue, which sources said was more than $100,000 apiece.
Trump had raged earlier this month after the New York Times reported that the duo, who hold top roles at the MAGA Inc super pac, had taken a trip to back a political party in the ethnically Serbian Republika Srpska, where they advised the victorious ruling party, led by Milorad Dodik, in the region’s election.
Dodik is friendly toward both Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The side job gave the impression that LaCivita and Blair were enriching themselves off their connection to Trump and taking their eyes off beleaguered Republican congressional campaigns — though some of their colleagues described them as remaining engaged remotely in the US election work.
“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them,” Trump fumed on Truth Social in his initial response on Oct. 7.
“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C. I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”
Blair, who masterminded a Republican redistricting drive this year to redraw House districts to favor the GOP, accompanied Trump to a campaign rally in South Carolina on Wednesday, indicating a thaw.
A White House official told The Post on Thursday that Trump did not seem to be upset with Blair or likely to blame him if Republicans are wiped out on Nov. 3, describing their conversations as businesslike and tactical.

articles.title_orig: Wealthy Chinese move offshore money to U.S. banks as Beijing’s tax net widens
articles.title_zh: Wealthy Chinese move offshore money to U.S. banks as Beijing’s tax net widens
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE —  Wealthy Chinese rattled by Beijing's widening hunt for overseas wealth are turning to a once-familiar refuge for their money: the U.S.
Private bankers and lawyers who work with Chinese clients say inquiries about opening U.S. bank accounts have grown in the months after Beijing imposed retroactive taxes on offshore wealth in July, moving assets previously stored in Singapore or Hong Kong there to stay further away from Beijing's reach.
"It has become relatively prevalent," said Keith Tan, CEO of Singapore-based Golden Acacia Capital, who is helping Chinese clients manage their offshore portfolios. His clients began planning exits to the U.S. in July, and some have the accounts set up in less than two months. "The hurdle is not that high for Chinese clients to open American accounts and transfer assets there."
Wealthy clients tend to choose large private banks while smaller accounts go to regional banks or online brokers, Tan said.
The rush has gained urgency with China's new tax regime on offshore trusts. Authorities said in July that income and gains from overseas trusts owned by Chinese tax residents would be taxed at 20%, setting off a scramble for cash and alternative structures .
Lawyers in Singapore and Hong Kong have been working to tally how much tax their clients owe, facilitating trusts' unwinding, sales of shares in listed companies or applying for loans to meet the outsized tax bill.
Meanwhile, the U.S. sits outside the Common Reporting Standard, or CRS, the OECD framework under which more than 100 jurisdictions automatically share financial account data. While banks in Singapore and Hong Kong are supposed to report China-linked accounts to Beijing, American banks have no such obligation.
Non-resident clients who open foreign bank accounts in the U.S. can also find investment vehicles with reduced or no tax-filing obligations to the Internal Revenue Service, said James Wang, CEO of Blue Brick Consulting Group, a private-client tax advisor. But China's latest regulations require people classified as Chinese tax residents to self-declare worldwide income to Beijing, Wang said.
Banks in New York are seizing the opportunity to offer a solution that could shield Chinese customers from their country's tax man. U.S. banks are straining to keep up with the rise in demand, according to a New York-based wealth-planning advisor who works with Chinese family offices.
"With inquiries surging, some banks have shortened the timeframe for clients to meet required minimum capital commitments" before the accounts are subject to closure, said the advisor, who requested anonymity to speak about bank processes.
Chinese families with offspring holding U.S. green cards have also used foreign grantor trusts – structures treated as owned by their non-American founder – to shield them from some tax exposure in the U.S., Tan said. Low-tax states such as Nevada and Florida have become popular choices, he added.
"They are gambling on not being disclosed, because the U.S. does not share information as part of the CRS system; they can dodge tax authorities," said Clifford Ng, a partner at Zhong Lun law firm in Hong Kong. Ng also expects that some with Hong Kong or Singapore residency whose trusts have not yet been flagged to Beijing may unwind those structures and transfer the money out.
Lawyers caution that though the route works for now to avoid disclosure, it may be temporary. Money held offshore has probably already been reported to Beijing through the CRS and would "have shown up in China at some point," Ng said, so a transfer from a Singapore or Hong Kong bank to a U.S. one would be visible on its way out.
"They may still be in breach of the rules because they have an undisclosed offshore account that's making money and they're not declaring it onshore," Ng said. "Hiding is not tax planning."
Washington's Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act requires foreign banks to report American clients, but so far there's no matching automatic flow from U.S. banks to Beijing.
Cris Cao, Beijing-based partner at W&H Law Firm, agreed on the risk of Beijing's ability to tax money moved to the U.S. "Even if they move all the money out of the CRS-reported accounts and into U.S. bank accounts, that doesn't naturally reduce or wipe out the tax authorities' right to tax, or their obligation to pay," he said.
"There was a record of it being transferred out," Cao said, and "that alone is enough for the tax authorities to levy tax."
What's more, the window of opportunity may have closed. Moving money that is already offshore around is relatively easy, but getting capital out of mainland China has become increasingly difficult.
"Nearly no sizeable money onshore will be able to leave the country from now on," said Jingkuan Lin, a private banker at Bank of Singapore, who sees the offshore banking industry being further limited to serving the existing pool of capital outside China.

articles.title_zh: Rare unrest flares in Tunisian capital as police clash with protesters
articles.content_orig:
Tunisian police have clashed with protesters in rare unrest in the capital city of Tunis, as well as ⁠⁠in the southern town of Jebiniana, over recent deaths linked to the police.
Police forces fired tear gas on Thursday to disperse protesters in ⁠⁠Ettadhamen, a suburb ⁠⁠of the capital, following the death of a man detained on suspicion of drug dealing.
The man’s family said he died as a result of abuse by police officers after his arrest, ‌‌calling for the circumstances of his death to be clarified and those responsible to be held accountable.
Local media, however, reported that he died after swallowing drugs.
Protesters blocked roads, burned tyres and threw stones at police. Security forces responded by firing tear gas while seeking ⁠⁠to secure a National Guard station in ⁠⁠the area, the Reuters news agency reported.
In Jebiniana, in Sfax governorate, police clashed with protesters following the death of a man whose relatives said he had died while being chased by security forces.
Tunisian media reported that protesters set a vehicle ablaze and burned tyres, while police used tear gas against the protesters.
Students in the coastal city of Sfax protested another civilian death, this time blaming ambulance services for the death of a female student who suffered a cardiac problem.
Her colleagues said ambulance personnel took too long to arrive, citing a lack of medical facilities, and ‌‌called for a strike at Sfax University’s faculties on Friday.
The flare-ups on Thursday coincide with a deepening economic, social and political crisis in Tunisia, heightening ⁠⁠fears of a wider wave of violent protests as anger grows over deteriorating living conditions and poor public services.
Thousands of Tunisians joined the largest protest against President Kais Saied in years in the ‌‌capital ‌‌on Saturday, accusing him of undermining democracy and mishandling the economy in a growing challenge to his rule.
A Tunisian military court on Wednesday sentenced opposition ⁠⁠politician Olfa ⁠⁠Hamdi to four years in prison on charges of plotting against state security and inciting the ⁠⁠military to disobey orders, the latest move against opponents of ⁠⁠Saied.

articles.content_orig:
AstraZeneca moves to make the lung cancer treatment available in the US after lengthy delays raised concerns over patient access
Global pharmaceutical firm AstraZeneca said on Thursday it would start selling a cancer drug after coming under criticism for failing to bring it to the US market faster, prompting some Americans to fly to Shanghai to procure the potentially life-saving medicine first developed by China.
In recent months, desperate Americans have travelled to China to obtain the Chinese-made cancer drug that was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration but remained unavailable in the country for more than a year, according to a cancer-treatment awareness advocate who made the journey while his mother was battling the disease.
Developed by China’s Dizal Pharmaceutical, sunvozertinib is a targeted lung cancer drug designed to treat adults with an advanced form of the illness, offering another treatment option for patients.
“The drug was approved in China in 2023. The FDA approved it in July 2025,” Max Doppelt, chief executive of Patient Data Vault, a consultancy that connects cancer patients to clinical trials, wrote on social media on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Moderna, Merck shares fall on eagerly anticipated cancer vaccine results
articles.title_zh: Moderna, Merck shares fall on eagerly anticipated cancer vaccine results
articles.content_orig:
A regimen involving the vaccine cut the risk of relapse or death by 42% in a landmark melanoma study that met investor expectations but triggered a “sell-the-news” response, one analyst wrote.
A cancer vaccine developed by Moderna and Merck & Co. has lived up to its billing, meeting lofty expectations from industry watchers and physicians in slowing the return of advanced melanoma, according to data published ahead of a major medical meeting.
Moderna and Merck reported in August that a combination of the vaccine, “intismeran autogene,” and Merck’s immunotherapy Keytruda, bested Keytruda alone in a late-stage trial. That study evaluated both regimens in the “adjuvant” setting after surgical removal of a tumor.
The companies didn’t disclose details from the trial at the time, only noting that the combination had met its main goal at an early, pre-planned data check. Nonetheless, the results were hailed by analysts as a “landmark moment” and evidence that intismeran is destined for billions of dollars in sales. Moderna’s stock price swelled more than four-fold afterwards.
The announcement made a coming Saturday presentation from the trial at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting this year one of the biotechnology sector’s most eagerly anticipated. Ahead of it, Wall Street investors expected the intismeran regimen to be associated with anywhere from 40% to 50% relative reduction in the risk of disease recurrence or death.
Moderna had already stated a 35% lowering would constitute a clinically significant outcome, which itself was a high bar considering Keytruda alone hit the 43% mark when compared to a placebo.
Screenshots of the findings were leaked on social media Thursday, prompting ESMO to immediately release the closely guarded study details before the meeting. According to those findings, intismeran met its mark, as the combination cut the relative risk of disease recurrence or death by 42% compared to Keytruda alone after a median of 24.6 months.
The results fall a touch short of the 44% figure initially observed in a smaller and similarly closely watched Phase 2 trial. Long-term results from that study were even more profound, showing that the risk of relapse was nearly cut in half after five years of follow-up.
Shares of both companies immediately fell on the news, with Moderna’s stock price tumbling by nearly 25% and Merck’s by around 1%.
Some analysts immediately rallied to both companies’ defense. A “sell-the-news reaction is playing out,” wrote William Blair analyst Myles Minter. The findings "represent a highly compelling efficacy profile and substantially clear the [physician]-defined bar for a practice-changing dataset in adjuvant melanoma,” added TD Cowen analyst Tyler Van Buren.
RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh, however, noted that the results were on the “low end” of expectations and showed a "deterioration" from what was seen in earlier testing.
“While approval seems likely, commercial success is far less certain,” Huynh wrote.
Investigators interviewed by BioPharma Dive argued that the data represent a possible step forward in care for a persistent type of cancer.
Even with the availability of Keytruda — one of the most successful cancer drugs in history — one-third or more of people diagnosed with late-stage melanoma will die or see their disease return within five years of treatment. Drugmakers have struggled mightily to improve upon those numbers, with “PD-1” inhibitors like Keytruda as well as other medications.
“We have tried really hard. I have led clinical trials. None of them has improved over PD-1,” said Hussein Tawbi, a professor of medicine at the MD Anderson Cancer Center and an investigator in Moderna and Merck’s study. “We were resigned to the fact that this was the best we can do for patients. And now we see we can do better.”
Adding intismeran to Keytruda also reduced the relative risk of cancer spreading to “distant” organs or tissues by 38% versus Keytruda alone, researchers found.
The trial enrollees who got intismeran reported similar rates of side effects, although those recipients had a substantially higher frequency of fever and injection-site pain. About 7% of the people who got intismeran discontinued treatment because of an adverse event, compared with 5% of those in the comparator group.
The risk of these side effects is likely “something a lot of patients would be willing to take on” given their chance to live longer, said Janice Mehnert, director of melanoma and cutaneous medical oncology at NYU Langone Health. Mehnert was also involved in the study.
The results are the product of decades of research into vaccines that can train the body’s immune system to better recognize and hunt down cancer cells. Several earlier projects failed because they didn’t trigger a strong enough immune response, stimulated the wrong immune cells or couldn’t overcome tumors’ ability to thwart the body’s defenses. But more recently, developers like Moderna have turned to mRNA technology popularized by COVID-19 vaccines to come up with a newer approach.
This strategy is known as “individualized neoantigen therapy.” It involves sequencing a patient’s tumor to find cancer-specific protein flags, or “neoantigens,” and then delivering into cells mRNA that encodes for them. Their presence sparks a response from immune defenders called T cells to hunt down and destroy any cells with those proteins.
Intismeran teaches the body to spot up to 34 neoantigens. Another developer, BioNTech, has an individualized therapy in testing in colorectal and pancreatic cancer.
Moderna and Merck have now shown the approach can work in melanoma. But physicians and investors aren’t yet sure how broadly impactful it might be in other types of cancer or in earlier stage disease. BioNTech recently reported that its personalized vaccine failed a mid-stage trial in colorectal cancer.
Merck and Moderna are running additional studies in lung, bladder and kidney cancer. Interim results from a mid-stage trial in kidney tumors could come later this year or in the first half of 2027, RBC analyst Huynh recently wrote in a note to investors.

articles.title_orig: Macron blames ‘seditious’ far left for unrest as France bans some protests
articles.title_zh: Macron blames ‘seditious’ far left for unrest as France bans some protests
articles.content_orig:
French authorities have barred demonstrations in several of the country’s largest cities, as President Emmanuel Macron blamed far-left groups for stoking violence during weekend protests .
The Paris Police Prefecture announced that Thursday’s protests would be banned in key parts of the city until 8pm (18:00 GMT). That includes areas near the presidential Elysee Palace, both houses of parliament, the city’s main train stations, as well as parts of downtown where looting occurred over the weekend.
A police source told the AFP news agency the ban was necessary due to organisers’ “inability to prevent violence and vandalism”.
Elsewhere in France, authorities also prohibited protests planned for Thursday in Lyon, Lille and Grenoble.
The restrictions come after more than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday in a protest that brought together students demanding better conditions in schools and groups denouncing high living costs.
France’s ⁠justice minister Gerald Darmanin said on Thursday that at least 2,700 people had been taken into custody after riots broke out in several areas , and shops were looted. Darmanin added that 217 of those arrested had already been convicted and jailed. 1,000 others were being prosecuted.
President Macron blamed Saturday’s riots on what he called “seditious acts” by “ultra-left” groups, whom he accused of trying to “bring down the Republic”.
Speaking from the Elysee Palace on Thursday, Macron said France would ban all “illegitimate” protests in the coming days, while approved demonstrations led by organised groups like unions would be required to take alternative routes outside city centres to protect businesses .
He added that he would convene the country’s defence council on Friday to take further action.
Thursday’s planned protests were seen as a prelude to a large demonstration on Saturday, when activists from the “yellow vest” movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, are expected to join.
Some of those protests, including marches in Lyon, will also be banned, local authorities said after hours of “chaos” last weekend when more than 200 shops were looted.
Officials for the Bouche-du-Rhone region covering France’s second-largest city Marseille has also banned all protests there on Saturday citing “obvious reasons of security”.
The French government said the Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in Paris would remain closed on Saturday due to new planned demonstrations.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, a far-left candidate for next year’s presidential election criticised by the government for not strongly condemning the protest violence, blamed authorities’ “non-stop brutal repression” for the unrest.
“On Saturday, the army is guarding buildings instead of the police, and the Paris police prefect is asking shopkeepers to call on private security guards…,” Melenchon said in a post on X.
Meanwhile Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader currently topping opinion polls, accused Macron’s government of being too soft and lacking authority.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a “massive” security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures.
Meanwhile, Macron held a meeting with intelligence services, Lecornu and ministers on Thursday morning to obtain a detailed account of what went wrong over the weekend and review preparations for upcoming protests.
Union representatives said their meeting with Lecornu did not result in concrete proposals. They are now focusing on another big day of action scheduled for November 5, calling on private and public sector employees to join.
The education demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of staff.
From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, including in smaller towns.
High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods.
The school demonstrations and blockades have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs.

Two months ago, Moderna's ( MRNA ) melanoma vaccine handed the stock its best day ever. Now leaked results from the same trial have handed it its biggest intraday drop on record.
The stock fell as much as 26% before closing down more than 17%. That's still its worst day since Aug. 20, the session right after its best day.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
More than $17 billion in market value has vanished as details from the late-stage trial circulated ahead of their official debut . Merck ( MRK ), Moderna's partner on the vaccine, confirmed the results came out early. The full data is set for release Saturday at Europe's biggest cancer conference, in Madrid.
The leaked numbers are still good. The personalized vaccine, paired with Merck's blockbuster Keytruda, reportedly cut the risk of the cancer returning or death by 42%. An earlier, smaller trial showed 49%, though it used different patients, so it isn't a direct comparison. The bigger issue is how much the stock had already run, nearly quadrupling from mid-August to Wednesday.
Merck fell nearly 4% at its low before paring more than half the drop. The vaccine is central to Moderna's story, but it's just an add-on for Merck.
The rest of healthcare is rallied. Eli Lilly ( LLY ) is added more than $33 billion in market value, about twice what Moderna lost. Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) and Pfizer ( PFE ) rose, too.
The iShares Biotechnology ETF ( IBB ) and SPDR S&P Biotech ETF ( XBI ) were only modestly lower, roughly in step with the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).
On Aug. 19, Moderna rocketed 177% to close at $174.38 after the company said the trial met its goals. It kept climbing from there, and on Wednesday, it posted its highest close since December 2021.
Thursday's low came within 4% of that August close before buyers stepped in. A sustained break below $174 would put $116 in focus. That's where trading opened on the record day.

It is a bitter moment for the Palestinian citizens of Israel who will go to the polls on Tuesday. We are part of a national election in a state that is practicing the most devastating war, ethnic cleansing and violence against our people since the Nakba of 1948. Insecurity, after all, changes the meaning of political participation.
The attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, the war in Gaza and the political transformation inside Israel have forever altered the relationship among Palestinian citizens of Israel, the state and the Palestinian national question. Palestinian citizens are not only citizens of Israel; they are part of the larger Palestinian people whose experience over the past three years cannot be separated from what happens inside Israel.
Being a Palestinian Israeli voter is a paradox: We are asked to participate in a political system that does not treat us as an equal part of that democracy. Many of Israel’s political parties, including those seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, continue to resist the idea of an Arab party participating in a governing coalition. At the same time, some of them also understand that a high Palestinian turnout could help change the government .
In other words, our vote is important enough to affect the future of Israel, but most of the candidates still consider us to be unacceptable partners in governing. These questions became particularly urgent in September when Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify the two Arab-majority parties from participating in this election. The Supreme Court overturned the decision, allowing them to run, though one candidate, Sami Abu Shehadeh, withdrew his candidacy after a public campaign against him.
Amid all of this, the daily lives of Palestinian citizens of Israel are growing more precarious. In recent years, organized crime has transformed life in many Palestinian communities: In 2025, 252 Arab citizens were killed in violent crimes — a record high. For many, the recent spike in crime is not simply experienced as a failure of policing. It is also seen as an expression of unequal citizenship and racist policies that exacerbate a long-held sense of state-led mistreatment. In the best case, we are seen as second- or third-class citizens; in the worst, we are enemies. The experience of abandonment is real.

Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios.
Why it matters: AI agents are becoming a nightmare for America's banks, making their way into banking systems faster than financial institutions can respond.
Driving the news: Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and others are racing to contain agent risks. Some are aware of unauthorized access, people familiar with the issue said.
What they're saying: Bank executives described the situation as horrifying, with one official saying the industry has grave concerns about agents gaining access to customer accounts and taking steps that could impact user finances.
State of play: The concerns are at the root of the decision by several banks to restrict third-party AI agent access, the people said.
Zoom out: Most banks have authorized or are moving in the direction of allowing read-only access , which should allow agents to see customer financial information without taking action.
Reality check: Several industry and bank executives told Axios they recognize the need to find a middle-ground with AI agents.
Threat level: Many banks are broadly not able to parse whether agent account activity is user-directed, sources said.
What we're watching: On one hand, banks are best positioned to respond to the threats and opportunities of AI given their cash on hand and experience as critical infrastructure.
The bottom line: The rapid pace of AI advancement is becoming a security nightmare for America's financial institutions.

articles.title_zh: Microsoft Says Its New AI Is More Than Twice as Good at Diagnosing Diseases as Doctors
articles.content_orig:
‘We’re going to build something that is indistinguishable from human performance … in the next couple of years,’ Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge.
‘We’re going to build something that is indistinguishable from human performance … in the next couple of years,’ Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge.
For years, AI leaders have touted healthcare as one of the clearest examples of where their technology will improve lives. Now “it is finally here,” Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge . The company claims to have developed an AI-powered tool it says can diagnose conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors.
The findings, published Thursday in one of the world’s most prestigious journals, Science , are based on tests pitting Microsoft’s AI system against human physicians on a series of scenarios drawn from medical case reports and emergency department data. Microsoft compiled the cases into its own benchmark, SDBench, which it plans to open-source. Designed to function like a panel of medical experts, Microsoft’s Diagnostic Orchestrator uses multiple AI agents to reason through symptoms and medical histories, decide what tests to order, and arrive at a diagnosis, mimicking the process doctors use to investigate cases.
On cases taken from hundreds of reports published in The New England Journal of Medicine , Microsoft’s system achieved a diagnostic accuracy of around 83 percent, compared with roughly 36 percent for generalist physicians using references and 22 percent for those working without them. The Diagnostic Orchestrator also outperformed doctors on emergency department cases drawn from a large database of patient admissions at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, scoring 80 percent accuracy compared with an average of 47 percent for human physicians. The AI system also tended to reach its diagnoses at a lower estimated cost than human counterparts.
The researchers say that the system, which is powered by OpenAI’s GPT-5, also outperformed frontier AI models operating on their own, though the peer-reviewed paper does not include newer models like GPT-6 Astra , Meta’s Muse Wonder Full , Google’s Gemini 4 Argon , or Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 . The Diagnostic Orchestrator was first developed when GPT-4.1 was the most advanced model available, but the researchers say subsequent testing suggests that “improvements in model capability do not necessarily diminish the benefits” of having multiple agents work together.
Microsoft acknowledges there’s a long road ahead before the technology can be widely deployed. While the tests more closely mirror the way doctors diagnose conditions — asking questions, weighing possible explanations, and ordering tests before reaching a diagnosis — the system has only been tested on past medical cases and it remains unclear how well it would perform in real clinical settings. “It needs clinical validation,” Suleyman says. “That is a leap, but this is a major milestone along that journey.”
The research is part of a broader ambition at Microsoft to develop what the company calls “medical superintelligence” — AI that can outperform the best human-led healthcare systems. Microsoft has used the term “superintelligence” since before Donald Trump and his administration co-opted it as a catch-all replacement for “AI.”
Diagnosis is just part of Microsoft’s health vision, says the company’s AI health lead, Dr. Dominic King, a coauthor of the study. In a blog post published Thursday and an article in the BMJ Digital Health & AI medical journal, the company outlines five other areas it believes AI will need to master, including coordinating clinical care, making treatment decisions, and handling the human side of medicine.
King tells The Verge that Microsoft plans to begin testing the system in hospital settings with the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center to see how it performs in real-world clinical environments. Neither King nor Suleyman would commit to a firm timeline, though King says it will likely “get underway in the next couple of months.”
Commercialization could also be on the horizon, though Microsoft has yet to say when or how the technology might become available. The company already has a significant presence in US healthcare through its digital tools, and health is one of the most popular uses for its consumer-facing chatbot Copilot . King emphasizes the need for a responsible rollout, noting the high regulatory and compliance requirements in medicine that would need to be followed.
“Next year we’re going to see extremely impressive deployments of intelligent systems in production,” Suleyman says. “I think that this is just going to change the way care is delivered in a big way.”
Suleyman has spoken previously about his “human-centered” vision for AI, and said medicine is no exception. Even as he predicts the arrival of “something that is indistinguishable from human performance on medical superintelligence in the next couple of years,” he insists that human clinicians should and will always have a central role in patient care.
While he acknowledges AI could end up with doctors being handed more work, he says his hope is that it will take some of “the drudgery” out of medicine, freeing up clinicians to spend more time with patients.
“I’m very optimistic about what’s coming next,” he says. “I think this is why we build technology.”

articles.title_orig: Moderna stock crashes as leaked melanoma data threatens its record August rally
articles.title_zh: Moderna stock crashes as leaked melanoma data threatens its record August rally
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Two months ago, Moderna's ( MRNA ) melanoma vaccine handed the stock its best day ever. Now leaked results from the same trial have handed it its biggest intraday drop on record.
The stock fell as much as 26% before closing down more than 17%. That's still its worst day since Aug. 20, the session right after its best day.
More than $17 billion in market value has vanished as details from the late-stage trial circulated ahead of their official debut . Merck ( MRK ), Moderna's partner on the vaccine, confirmed the results came out early. The full data is set for release Saturday at Europe's biggest cancer conference, in Madrid.
The leaked numbers are still good. The personalized vaccine, paired with Merck's blockbuster Keytruda, reportedly cut the risk of the cancer returning or death by 42%. An earlier, smaller trial showed 49%, though it used different patients, so it isn't a direct comparison. The bigger issue is how much the stock had already run, nearly quadrupling from mid-August to Wednesday.
Merck fell nearly 4% at its low before paring more than half the drop. The vaccine is central to Moderna's story, but it's just an add-on for Merck.
The rest of healthcare is rallied. Eli Lilly ( LLY ) is added more than $33 billion in market value, about twice what Moderna lost. Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) and Pfizer ( PFE ) rose, too.
The iShares Biotechnology ETF ( IBB ) and SPDR S&P Biotech ETF ( XBI ) were only modestly lower, roughly in step with the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).
On Aug. 19, Moderna rocketed 177% to close at $174.38 after the company said the trial met its goals. It kept climbing from there, and on Wednesday, it posted its highest close since December 2021.
Thursday's low came within 4% of that August close before buyers stepped in. A sustained break below $174 would put $116 in focus. That's where trading opened on the record day.

articles.title_orig: U.S. 10-Year Treasury Yield Falls Under 5% as French Turmoil Fuels Flight for Safety
articles.title_zh: U.S. 10-Year Treasury Yield Falls Under 5% as French Turmoil Fuels Flight for Safety
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices.
The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
"It is a flight to safety," said Mitch Goldberg, president of ClientFirst Strategy. "People are all of a sudden terrified of the amount of bond issuance by AI-related companies. They see the rates going up and people want to hold on to something that they think will be there at maturity."
Others on Wall Street also sought to explain the turnaround in bond prices.
"For the first time in a while, Treasurys are enjoying haven status," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds. "You have weakness in tech, an escalation of risk in the Middle East and higher oil. On a relative basis Treasurys start to look like the safe place to hide again in the short term."
The reversal in bonds this week emerged as questions persisted about the billions being spent to build artificial intelligence networks.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that while demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ," capital was scarce. Neoclouds are a specialized cloud computing providers that focus on high-performance tech infrastructure designed specifically for artificial intelligence.
This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades amid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices.
Above 5%, however, attitudes began to shift and yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%.
Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday. Oil prices moved sharply higher, with West Texas Intermediate futures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel. Brent crude futures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel.
Higher energy prices followed a New York Times report, citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"You always look for one risk point, and there isn't really just one at the moment, which makes it a little bit more challenging," said Gregory Faranello, head of U.S. macro strategy at South Street Securities. "But if I had to take one of those and say what's most important right now, it has to be what's going on geopolitically."
"The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. If energy prices "stay elevated, it could force the Fed's hand to do even more, which certainly wouldn't be wouldn't be a good thing for the bond market."

articles.title_orig: Taco Bell sticks with Pepsi as sister chain switches to Coke
articles.title_zh: Taco Bell sticks with Pepsi as sister chain switches to Coke
articles.content_orig:
PepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their long-running partnership through 2036, the food and beverage company said Thursday.
The announcement comes one week after Taco Bell's sister chain, KFC, said that it will switch to Coca-Cola as its U.S. beverage supplier. While it is unusual for large restaurant chains to change drink providers, the move is not unprecedented, as Coke and Pepsi try to win contracts through perks and other inducements.
Coke's win over Pepsi was more symbolic, representing another example of how the Atlanta-based company has been beating its rival in the soda category.
Pepsi's relationship with Taco Bell and KFC parent Yum Brands spans decades, back to when the beverage giant owned the restaurant chains before spinning them into a separate public company in 1997. Despite KFC's defection in the U.S., Pepsi remains an important partner for Yum and the chain's international markets, KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo on Oct. 15 that was obtained by CNBC.
Thanks to its partnership with Pepsi, Taco Bell has long served exclusive menu items that use Pepsi products, like Mountain Dew Baja Blast and Doritos Locos Tacos, at its restaurants.
The renewed deal also means that Taco Bell international markets such as Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Thailand will serve Pepsi products.

Blu-ray is fading after 20 years in the market, with Sony Japan finally discontinuing its last dedicated Blu-ray player. According to FlatpanelsHD , Sony Japan has finally marked the UBP-X700/K player as “Discontinued,” meaning customers in the country can no longer purchase a new standalone Blu-ray player from the company. This should not come as a surprise, as Sony stopped shipping the players in February of this year, suggesting that Sony only relied on existing inventory for its remaining Blu-ray player sales.
The PlayStation 5 is the only remaining Sony device that can play Blu-ray discs, but the company has also announced that it will end physical game disc production by January 2028. Because of this, some people fear that the upcoming PlayStation 6 will no longer have an optical drive. This move follows in the footsteps of LG , which ended Blu-ray player production in 2024. Japanese electronics companies Elecom and Buffalo have also ended production of Blu-ray drives for PCs this year, although Buffalo Americas says that it is “fully committed to supplying optical drives to the American market, and our DVD/Blu-ray drive products are anticipated to remain available for the near future.”
This move away from physical media and focus on streaming is worrying, especially to those who are concerned that we are moving towards a world where people no longer own anything. Because of this, sales of “retro media,” including CDs and vinyl, went up by 59% and 18% respectively . While you could still purchase a Blu-ray player from other manufacturers like Panasonic, Sony is one of the bigger companies that built and supported the standard, and its move to end the production and sale of Blu-ray players will leave this niche market even smaller. The audiophile market is facing the same dilemma, as some Hi-Fi player manufacturers ended production of selected products because optical drive makers have stopped making the components needed to read SACDs .
Ultra HD Blu-ray is facing the same upheaval that VHS and DVDs went through with the introduction of new formats. But while the older technologies were replaced by higher-quality formats, Blu-ray is being replaced not by more pixels, but by the convenience of streaming. However, it also comes with the caveat that people would no longer own physical media; a trend that worries data archivists.

articles.title_orig: TV Reporter, Bystander Save Man From Sinking Car
articles.title_zh: TV Reporter, Bystander Save Man From Sinking Car
articles.content_orig:
A driver has been rescued by two bystanders, including an ABC reporter, from his sinking car in floodwater north of Brisbane.
The man drove his four-wheel-drive at speed through water on Buchanan Road at Morayfield.
The car stalled and started to sink.
ABC reporter Will Murray swimming to the sinking car. ( ABC News )
ABC reporter Will Murray and Daniel Hainey swam out to the car and pulled the driver out of the vehicle.
About 170 millimetres of rain has fallen in the area since this morning.
Speaking after a shower and some lunch, Murray said he was relieved everyone was OK.
"I saw him drive in and immediately his car started floating downstream so I rang Triple Zero," he said.
"On the phone the operator asked me if I could see the driver and if I thought he could get free.
"Initially I could see him, but he disappeared from my sight within seconds so I made the call to jump in."
Murray said he handed the phone to his colleague, camera operator Liz Pickering, and started swimming towards the sinking car.
The two rescuers pulled the man from the car just before it went under water. ( ABC News )
"When we got to the car we tried to open the closest door, no luck, then got on the back of the car with the thought to break the back window," he said.
"I thought to try the passenger side rear door first and put my feet against the car and pulled as hard as I could and with some luck the door swung open.
"I think water rushing in helped create some pressure to force the door open."
Murray said the driver was then able to make his way to the open door, and the rescuers pulled him to safety and shallow waters.
"All three of us gave each other a big hug and were just so relieved," he said.
"It was very scary, but happy everyone is safe and relieved it is OK.
"I just witnessed how quickly it can go south and it is terrifying. Please don't drive into floodwaters."
Mr Hainey, who rescued the man alongside Murray, said he was out with his family when he saw the ute but did not realise someone was inside until the window moved.
"The car began to slowly sink deeper and deeper, and that's when I thought, 'Oh no, this is not looking good', so I started swimming in there," he said.
Mr Hainey said the driver was "very, very lucky".
The Queensland Fire Department advises all residents not to swim in floodwater.
Pickering was on scene filming overlay footage of the flooded road when the incident occurred.
She captured the incident on video as the men rescued the driver from the vehicle.
ABC reporter Will Murray and another man pull a man from a sinking car. ( ABC News )
Murray said emergency services arrived about 10 minutes after the rescue.
"We were chatting with the man and he was saying he didn't see the signage and didn't realise how deep it was," Murray said.
"I had no idea how deep it was and that's the lesson we keep hearing, isn't it, that you can't tell and you really couldn't; it didn't look particularly severe.
"But as you can see in the vision, the car completely disappears, it's clearly very deep in the middle there."
Speaking about being called a hero or a lifesaver, Murray quickly diverted attention to the men and women who work for emergency services.
He said he has a greater respect for the work they do.
"The adrenaline is still very, very high. I don't know how people do this regularly," he said.

The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield.
Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supported Houthis in Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. The state department spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.”
The state department said the order covered its embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the US war on Iran and had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although in recent weeks some diplomats had returned.
Media outlets – including NBC and AFP – reported that families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, while the New York Times said the Trump administration was developing plans to restart the war on Iran.
However, in his statement on Wednesday, Pigott described the reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate” and said the state department order was for the departure of staff and their families from Saudi Arabia only.
Saudi Arabia has faced a succession of deadly attacks from the Houthis over recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport which was the kingdom’s deadliest in years as the war with the group escalates.
On Thursday the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced that two people had been killed in overnight attacks on King Fahd international airport in Dammam on the Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
Eight people were injured and there was material damage to the airport, according to officials. The global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said flights had been diverted away from the airport.
Separately, falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility in the country’s south-east killed two people and injured a further two, the Saudi energy ministry said.
The Houthis said on Thursday ⁠they ⁠had ​launched attacks on ⁠Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry in ⁠Riyadh, Saudi ​Aramco ‌facilities ‌in Yanbu ‌and King Fahd international airport in Dammam.
Essential workers at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in the east of the country were told to evacuate on Thursday, two sources told Agence France-Presse, after their non-essential colleagues were told to work from home since last week.
The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf in late February before the start of its war against Iran. NBC reported that the US military had been quietly scaling back its presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, but a spokesperson from US central command told the US news outlet that service members were regularly moved to “optimize mission readiness”.
The withdrawal of staff from the region coincides with reports that Trump has been presented with plans for restarting strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
The New York Times reported that the US and Israel had developed plans for a “short but intensive operation” after the defense secretary, Peter Hegseth, travelled to Israel earlier this week for meetings with the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Last week ⁠Trump said the US was hoping to knock out Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain , a site linked to the country’s ⁠nuclear program, however the US president has publicly said he does not intend to restart the war before the 3 November elections.
